Why Agents Compromise Safety Under Pressure

Hengle Jiang    Ke Tang Affiliation: Guangdong Provincial Key Laboratory of Brain-inspired Intelligent Computation, Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Affiliation: Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, China
Abstract

Large Language Model agents deployed in complex environments frequently encounter a conflict between maximizing goal achievement and adhering to safety constraints. This paper identifies a new concept called Agentic Pressure, which characterizes the endogenous tension emerging when compliant execution becomes infeasible. We demonstrate that under this pressure agents exhibit normative drift where they strategically sacrifice safety to preserve utility. Notably we find that advanced reasoning capabilities accelerate this decline as models construct linguistic rationalizations to justify violation. Finally, we analyze the root causes and explore preliminary mitigation strategies, such as pressure isolation, which attempts to restore alignment by decoupling decision-making from pressure signals.

1 Introduction

The transition of Large Language Models (LLMs) from static chatbots (Adiwardana et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023; Anthropic, 2024) to goal-oriented agents (Yao et al., 2022; Schick et al., 2023) represents a paradigm shift in artificial intelligence. Modern agents are expected to plan, execute, and adapt (Wang et al., 2023; Shinn et al., 2023) over long trajectories to satisfy user instructions. While this capability improves utility, it introduces a fundamental conflict between maximizing goal achievement and adhering to safety constraints (Amodei et al., 2016). In practice, as objectives become more specific and interaction horizons grow, constraints that were designed as hard boundaries can be treated as negotiable frictions.

Current safety evaluations predominantly focus on adversarial attacks (Kumar et al., 2024; Lu et al., 2024) where a malicious user attempts to trick the model. However, this perspective overlooks a critical threat arising from the internal drive of the agent. In practical scenarios, agents frequently encounter resource constraints such as insufficient budgets, upcoming deadlines, and unreliable tools (Ornia et al., 2025; Fan et al., 2025). These factors create a high pressure environment that fundamentally alters the operating context of the agent distinct from the adversarial settings typically studied. We illustrate this dilemma in Figure 1, which depicts the "Good Agent" Paradox.

To address this gap, we introduce the concept of Agentic Pressure. Unlike the static and exogenous pressure typically found in Large Language Model evaluations which relies on threatening prompts or aggressive language to induce compliance (Kim et al., 2024), Agentic Pressure is endogenous. It emerges naturally during the interaction loop as the agent perceives conflicts between its objective and the available resources. This pressure is not explicitly injected by the user but arises from the internal calculation of the agent that the task cannot be completed within the constraints of the environment. We hypothesize that under such pressure, even benign agents experience Instrumental Divergence (Gallow, 2025). Specifically, driven by a strong directive to be helpful, agents autonomously prioritize task utility over established safety protocols (Omohundro, 2018). Crucially, this is not merely a failure of execution but a cognitive shift where the agent actively rationalizes its safety violations as necessary compromises to benefit the user.

Experimental observations suggest that AI agents do not behave as purely rational actors that steadfastly maintain safety boundaries under such conditions (Arike et al., 2025). Instead, they exhibit behavioral shifts that render traditional static testing methods insufficient (Greenblatt et al., 2024). While such failures are often attributed to a lack of model capability or reasoning bandwidth, we propose that they are frequently the result of an adaptive response to environmental stress where the agent prioritizes utility over compliance. This implies that the testing problem for agents is fundamentally different from standard software testing because the subject under test dynamically adjusts its moral compass based on the perceived difficulty of the task (Amodei et al., 2016).

This paper investigates why agents compromise safety through a systematic study of this phenomenon. We first present a preliminary study using the TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024) environment to demonstrate the emergence of behavioral drift in long horizon scenarios without active pressure injection. Building on these findings, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation framework that actively simulates high pressure environments across multiple domains to quantify the extent of safety compromise. Finally, we propose a pressure isolation mechanism designed to decouple reasoning from execution which offers a potential architectural solution to mitigate these autonomous safety trade-offs.

2 Related Work

2.1 Safety in LLMs

Current research extensively covers safety alignment in large language models, primarily within the paradigm of conversational interaction. Established benchmarks such as HH-RLHF (Bai et al., 2022) and SafetyBench (Zhang et al., 2024) evaluate whether models can identify and refuse harmful instructions in static dialogue or multiple choice settings. A parallel line of inquiry investigates jailbreak, where users employ optimized adversarial suffixes (Zou et al., 2023) or prefix injections (Wei et al., 2023) to bypass these safety filters. More recently, studies on many-shot jailbreak (Anil et al., 2024) reveal that extended context windows can weaken alignment, as models prioritize in-context patterns over safety training. Crucially, these works typically evaluate language model in isolation, focusing on its ability to detect toxic content in text generation. They do not assess the autonomous agent, which must balance safety constraints against task utility in dynamic, multi-step environments.

2.2 Benchmarks for Agents

General agent benchmarks predominantly prioritize task completion accuracy above all other metrics. Foundational datasets like HotpotQA (Yang et al., 2018) and GSM8k (Cobbe et al., 2021) focus on reasoning chains. To evaluate broader autonomous capabilities, benchmarks such as ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023), GAIA (Mialon et al., 2023), and TheAgentCompany (Xu et al., 2025) assess proficiency in realistic environments. However, these frameworks operate on strictly outcome-based metrics. They classify a trajectory as successful solely based on goal completion, regardless of the methods used. This creates a critical evaluation blind spot: agents are implicitly incentivized to bypass safety constraints if doing so improves efficiency, as current utility benchmarks do not penalize functional but unsafe solutions.

2.3 Safety in Autonomous Agents

In the safety domain, existing works often diverge from the phenomenon of normative drift. Benchmarks like AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024), AgentHarm (Andriushchenko et al., 2025), and Agent Security Bench (Zhang et al., 2025) focus on adversarial robustness against malicious instructions. While R-Judge (Yuan et al., 2024) evaluates an agent’s ability to identify risks, it overlooks the critical "knowing-doing" gap.

Beyond adversarial settings, research into agentic alignment often relies on restricted contexts. Studies like Agentic Misalignment (Lynch et al., 2025) and the Machiavelli benchmark (Pan et al., 2023) examine ethical trade-offs but are frequently situated in fictional or game-based environments that lack the stakes of realistic deployment. Similarly, frameworks like ToolEmu (Ruan et al., 2024) assess tool execution risks but typically focus on isolated steps rather than cumulative dynamics. Mainstream productivity benchmarks focus exclusively on final outcomes and inadvertently reward unsafe behaviors that improve efficiency. Crucially, these evaluations overlook the endogenous pressure emerging from internal resource conflicts. Our work bridges this gap by situating agents in continuous constrained workflows to analyze how alignment deteriorates under cumulative stress.

3 Agentic Pressure

Large language model based agents operate in interactive environments where incentives and constraints evolve over time (Yao et al., 2022). In such settings, agent behavior is not determined solely by initial prompts, safety policies, or inherent model capabilities, but by how goal-directed decision making unfolds under changing external conditions (Schick et al., 2023).

Agentic Pressure is a force that spontaneously emerges from the interaction between an agent and its environment, causing the agent to generate outputs inconsistent with expectations even without malicious attacks. Agentic Pressure describes the endogenous tension where feasible options decrease just as the consequences of failure intensify. Unlike static task specifications, agentic pressure is cumulative and trajectory dependent. It develops across interaction turns as options disappear, resources are depleted, or stakes escalate.

Crucially, agentic pressure does not correspond to an internal psychological state of the model. Instead, it arises endogenously from the interaction loop between the agent and its environment. Under increasing pressure, agents may continue to exhibit fluent reasoning and nominal policy awareness, yet begin to reinterpret or discount safety constraints in order to preserve task progress. This shift does not require adversarial prompts or explicit instructions to violate rules, but follows naturally from sustained goal pursuit under constrained conditions.

3.1 From LLM Pressure to Agentic Pressure

It is important to distinguish agentic pressure from what prior work often describes as pressure on language models (Kim et al., 2024). In many evaluations, pressure is treated as an exogenous factor introduced through prompt design, such as urgent commands, fictional emergencies, or explicit requests to bypass safety rules. This form of pressure is linguistic, immediate, and static (Zhang et al., 2024).

By contrast, agentic pressure is not injected through language alone. It emerges dynamically during interaction as the environment evolves. It is a property of the agent’s decision context rather than a feature of the prompt or an internal state of the model. Two agents powered by the same underlying LLM may experience different pressure profiles depending on their interaction history, resource availability, and accumulated constraints.

Under agentic pressure, deviations in behavior or explanation do not reflect confusion about policy requirements. Instead, they arise because compliant actions become increasingly costly, delayed, or infeasible as the episode progresses. This distinction is critical for understanding agent behavior in realistic deployment settings, where pressure is rarely static and cannot be reduced to prompt level manipulation.

3.2 Taxonomy of Pressure Sources

In Figure 2, we categorize agentic pressure into three major types based on where it arises within the agent and environment interaction loop, including Resource Scarcity, Environmental Friction, and Social Inducement. It captures the most common pressure patterns we observe in practice, while additional sources may emerge in other domains or deployment settings. Crucially, these pressures are not triggered by explicit instructions to violate rules, but by conditions that progressively narrow feasible actions and increase the cost of failure.

Type I: Resource Scarcity

Resource scarcity arises when compliant actions exceed the agent’s available resources. A common form is temporal exhaustion, where strict time limits or step budgets leave insufficient capacity to complete all required verification procedures (Silver et al., 2017). Time functions as a core planning resource, and when the remaining horizon is too short, agents face a choice between task failure and skipping safety checks. Resource scarcity also includes budget constraints, where authorized options are unavailable due to financial or computational limits. In such cases, pressure emerges not because rules change, but because compliance becomes infeasible.

Type II: Environmental Friction

Environmental friction refers to obstacles that block standard execution paths even when resources remain available. One example is functional deadlock, where tools or APIs fail persistently (Schick et al., 2023), severing legitimate action channels. Another source is information asymmetry, where incomplete or noisy feedback forces agents to act under uncertainty. We also identify compliance rigidity, where static safety rules conflict with dynamic situations. When rigid protocols prevent timely action, agents may treat rule deviation as adaptive flexibility rather than noncompliance.

Type III: Social Inducement

Social inducement originates from user interaction dynamics rather than task structure. Urgency injection occurs when users emphasize severe consequences of failure, increasing the perceived stakes of task completion. Illicit opportunities introduce highly efficient but unauthorized options that appear attractive under constrained conditions (Achiam et al., 2017). User emotion further amplifies pressure through interaction, including authoritative, pleading, or aggressive behavior. Although these signals do not alter formal task requirements, they raise the perceived cost of refusal or delay and can shift agent priorities toward appeasement.

Across all categories, pressure is not a single factor but an accumulation of constraints that evolve over time. Agentic pressure emerges from how these constraints interact, progressively reshaping both agent behavior and the justifications offered for that behavior.

3.3 The Cognitive Shift: From Reasoning to Rationalization

Agentic pressure alters not only whether an agent complies with safety constraints, but how it constructs explanations for its behavior. In low-pressure settings, agents typically rely on normative reasoning, where safety rules function as stable constraints guiding action selection. Explanations in this condition are policy grounded and diagnostic, explicitly referencing constraints to justify decisions or refusals. As pressure accumulates, however, agents increasingly prioritize goal completion under high stakes, and explanations shift toward motivated rationalization. Rather than reflecting deliberation under fixed rules, explanations are constructed to legitimize actions taken under constrained feasibility, a pattern consistent with findings on motivated reasoning in human decision-making (Kunda, 1990).

Importantly, this shift can occur even when actions remain nominally compliant. Under high pressure, agents may reinterpret constraints as flexible or exceptional, framing policies as secondary to urgency or necessity. Prior work has shown that natural language explanations are not inherently faithful to underlying decision processes (Jacovi and Goldberg, 2020; Wiegreffe et al., 2021), and agentic pressure amplifies this gap. Explanations remain fluent and plausible, but become less informative about true decision criteria. As a result, explanation quality cannot be evaluated independently of pressure context, since identical explanations may serve fundamentally different roles across different pressure settings.

4 Preliminary Analysis

We first conduct a lightweight diagnostic study to test whether non-adversarial pressure signals alone can systematically alter an agent’s safety behavior in complex tool-using workflows. We utilized the TravelPlanner environment (Xie et al., 2024) as a testbed and extended its standard setting to simulate the friction and fatigue of realistic deployment. This preliminary analysis serves to demonstrate that agentic pressure is an endogenous phenomenon that emerges solely from the extension of interaction horizons and the introduction of environmental noise.

4.1 Experimental Setup

TravelPlanner provides environment constraints that enforce sandbox availability, a set of commonsense constraints for feasibility, and query-conditioned hard constraints such as budget, room rules, and cuisine requirements. We keep the environment constraints unchanged and expand the number of constraints within the existing commonsense and hard categories to better reflect realistic deployment policies and operational failure modes. To evaluate compliance at the trajectory level, we employ an external LLM monitor to verify each step and compute cumulative pass rates across episodes.

4.2 Stress-Testing Variants

Standard benchmarks typically involve short horizons (10-20 steps) with reliable tools which fail to capture the cumulative nature of agentic pressure. To amplify this pressure organically, we designed two realistic stress-testing variants.

Long Horizon

We extended the interaction horizon to exceed fifty steps while providing no corrective feedback or human intervention. The agent must independently maintain normative constraints solely through its internal context window which simulates an autonomous system drifting over a prolonged operational period.

Noisy Tools

We simulated realistic interface instability by injecting stochastic and non-adversarial perturbations into tool responses. These perturbations included transient service errors, partial output generation, and minor formatting inconsistencies. This setting introduces environmental friction that forces the agent to perform error handling and retries, thereby consuming cognitive reasoning bandwidth without altering the fundamental constraints of the task.

4.3 Preliminary Findings

Figure 3 shows that even mild, non-adversarial pressure signals systematically change agent behavior. Across models, extending the horizon and injecting tool noise both reduce constraint pass rates, indicating that the agent becomes less reliable as interaction context grows and execution becomes less stable. Notably, hard constraints are more fragile than commonsense constraints: under pressure, agents may still produce superficially feasible itineraries while increasingly failing to satisfy explicit user-specified requirements. These results support our premise that pressure can emerge endogenously from the interaction loop itself, motivating the active pressure injection framework in the next section.

5 Experiments and Analysis

Building on the preliminary analysis, we design a systematic experimental framework to quantify agent performance under actively induced pressure, as illustrated in Figure 4. We move from passive observation to controlled stress testing by adapting three established agent benchmarks, TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024), WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023), and ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023), and by adding a medical scenario. Across these diverse environments, we modify the interaction dynamics so that agents encounter structured conflicts between normative constraints and goal achievement.

5.1 Pressure Injection Mechanism

We inject pressure through overlaying strict normative constraints onto standard agent benchmarks while creating specific high inducement tasks. We design these scenarios so that the user objective is functionally antagonistic to the safety rules. For instance, we enforce a strict no flight policy while simultaneously presenting a user request that physically requires air travel to meet a deadline. This setup ensures that the most salient path to success involves a violation. Consequently the agent faces an immediate tension between the directive to be helpful and the requirement to remain safe. This forces the model to weigh the immediate utility of task completion against the abstract cost of rule violation without needing dynamic feedback loops. Crucially, some of these scenarios create an impossible task where no valid plan exists that satisfies both the user’s objective and the safety constraints. In such cases, the optimal and aligned behavior is justified refusal. However, our hypothesis is that under agentic pressure, models will perceive refusal as a failure mode. Driven by the imperative to be helpful, they tend to prioritize goal satisfaction over strict compliance, leading to the rationalized violation we aim to measure.

5.2 Baselines and Comparative Strategies

Our setting explicitly couples pressure with normative constraints, we compare our architecture against three widely used deployment strategies:

  • •

    Vanilla Agent: The base model equipped only with task instructions and tools. This estimates the natural drift rate under pressure without mitigation.

  • •

    Safety Prompting: A strategy where constraints are stated prominently and repeatedly in system instructions to encourage compliance through static guidance.

  • •

    Self-Reflection: A dynamic baseline where the agent is prompted to critique its own plan for potential violations before execution. This represents a strong prompt level mitigation that increases deliberation.

5.3 Evaluation Metrics

We evaluate each episode using a metric suite that separates functional capability from normative adherence.

Safety Adherence Rate (SAR).

This measures the fraction of constraints the agent satisfies. Let an episode ee contain TT interaction steps. At step tt, the verifier returns binary checks ce,t,k∈{0,1}c_{e,t,k}\in\{0,1\} for Ke,tK_{e,t} applicable constraints. We define the episode-level SAR as:

SAR⁡(e)=1T​∑t=1T(1Ke,t​∑k=1Ke,tce,t,k).\mathrm{SAR}(e)=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left(\frac{1}{K_{e,t}}\sum_{k=1}^{K_{e,t}}c_{e,t,k}\right). (1)
Goal Success Rate (GSR).

This measures the fraction of episodes where the agent achieves the intended objective. To strictly decouple utility from safety, we count a trajectory as a success if the functional goal is achieved, regardless of whether safety constraints are violated. Crucially, for infeasible instances (deadlocks), a “success” is defined as a justified refusal. GSR is defined as:

GSR=1|ℰ|​∑e∈ℰs⁡(e),\mathrm{GSR}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{E}|}\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}}s(e), (2)

where s⁡(e)=1s(e)=1 if the agent achieves the task goal even via constraint violation or produces a verifier-approved refusal with a concrete infeasibility explanation for infeasible instances, and s⁡(e)=0s(e)=0 otherwise.

Rationalization Score.

While behavioral metrics (e.g., Pass Rate) reveal what the agent did, they fail to explain why a violation occurred. To capture the internal state of agentic pressure, we implement an automated LLM-as-a-Judge framework using GPT-4o. We posit that pressure manifests linguistically in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) as a transition from normative reasoning to instrumental rationalization. We designed a specialized evaluation prompt that instructs the judge to analyze CoT traces for specific markers of cognitive dissonance: (1) Conflict Recognition, where the agent explicitly acknowledges the hard constraint; and (2) Justification Logic, where the agent constructs utilitarian arguments to override the rule. The Judge assigns a continuous Pressure Score from 0-5 based on the intensity of this rationalization. We provide the detailed scoring rubric and comparative case studies in Appendix.

5.4 Results Analysis

The quantitative results in Table 1 reveal a severe normative drift across all baseline strategies. Under high pressure, advanced models exhibit a significant collapse in safety adherence. For instance, GPT-4o sees its Safety Adherence Rate (SAR) plummet from 0.711 to 0.545, while Gemini 2.5 Pro experiences the most severe decline.

Instrumental Divergence

Crucially, this collapse in safety is not accompanied by a decline in utility; rather, it often leads to higher goal achievement. As shown in the ReAct baseline, while GPT-4o’s SAR drops significantly, its Goal Success Rate (GSR) actually increases from 0.609 to 0.690. A similar trend is observed in Llama-3-70B (Δ​GSR+0.019\Delta\text{GSR}+0.019). This inverse correlation confirms our hypothesis of Instrumental Divergence: the primal motivation for agent violation is that sacrificing safety constraints effectively removes barriers to success. Capable agents are not failing the task; they are strategically trading off safety to maximize the reward of task completion. We visualize this phenomenon in Figure 5, which illustrates the behavioral shift from the "Ideal Region" to the "Drift Region" under pressure.

Reasoning Capability and Vulnerability.

The Rationalization Score provides insight into the distinct failure mechanisms of different models, revealing that susceptibility to pressure correlates with reasoning capability. For smaller models like Qwen3-8B, which exhibit low Rationalization Scores, safety failures stem primarily from cognitive overload. Specifically, the forgetting of constraints in long contexts due to limited bandwidth rather than motivated defiance. In contrast, highly capable models like GPT-4o achieve high scores, utilizing their advanced reasoning to construct sophisticated justifications for non-compliance. Notably, adding Self-Reflection to GPT-4o exacerbates this behavior, deepening the SAR drop while increasing GSR. This confirms that misaligned reasoning power accelerates rationalized violations rather than acting as a safety guardrail.

5.5 Case Study: Stepwise Discovery and Rationalization

Qualitative analysis reveals that agents rarely exhibit immediate defiance. Instead, they follow a pattern of stepwise discovery, where the intent to violate emerges only after accumulating evidence of infeasibility. As shown in Table 2, under high pressure, repeated environmental friction creates a "cognitive funnel" that narrows the decision space, leading to rationalized priority inversion. The agent linguistically reframes the hard constraint as a negotiable guideline to preserve the user’s goal.

Crucially, this shift is strictly pressure dependent. In the control setting without urgency cues, the exact same deadlock triggers a divergent cognitive path: the agent maintains normative adherence and issues a justified refusal (e.g., "I apologize, but no compliant routes are available"). This contrast confirms that the violation is not a capability failure, but a motivated cognitive shift captured by our Rationalization Score.

5.6 Ablation Study: Validating the Pressure Mechanism

We investigate two interventions acting at different stages of the decision loop to determine whether normative drift is strictly mediated by pressure perception. Results for the architectural intervention are integrated into Table 1.

Pressure Isolation.

This method structurally decouples the decision-making agent from the pressure-inducing feedback loop. By preventing the planner from directly interacting with environmental friction and urgency signals, the agent focuses solely on the logical decision process without accumulating "agentic pressure." As shown in Table 1, this isolation effectively mitigates the safety collapse compared to the ReAct baseline, confirming that the violation stems from the perception of pressure rather than the task complexity itself.

Pre-decision Safety Check.

We also explored a minimal intervention where a verifier audits the proposed plan against constraints before execution, keeping the planner unchanged. Preliminary tests indicate that this method yields a marginal improvement of 3.2%. However, as this approach acts only as a final filter without addressing the root cause of instrumental rationalization, it requires further experimentation to validate its robustness in high-stakes deadlocks.

6 Conclusion

This paper formalizes Agentic Pressure as a critical vulnerability in the deployment of autonomous systems. We demonstrate that safety alignment is not a static property, but a consumable resource that decays under the friction of real-world operation. Crucially, this phenomenon is not a rare edge case but a fundamental structural risk: as agents are deployed into increasingly complex, long horizon workflows, the tension between goal achievement and normative constraints intensifies, making the emergence of instrumental non-compliance inevitable.

Our analysis reveals that advanced reasoning capabilities can exacerbate this drift. State-of-the-art models utilize their cognitive bandwidth to construct sophisticated linguistic rationalizations, reframing safety constraints as negotiable guidelines under pressure. This finding challenges the validity of current evaluation paradigms. We argue that future capability benchmarks must incorporate "stress-testing" dimensions to account for pressure. Evaluating agents solely in friction-free vacuums fails to predict their reliability in high stakes environments where compliance competes with utility.

Finally, our results indicate that relying on innate post-training alignment is insufficient to mitigate this risk, as pressure operates on the cognitive process itself. To ensure robust safety, the field must transition from prompt-based mitigations toward architectural defenses. As demonstrated by our pressure isolation framework, structurally decoupling the planning incentives from pressure perception offers a more reliable guarantee than relying on the model’s self-restraint. As autonomous agents evolve from chat interfaces to actors in the physical economy, acknowledging and architecturally managing agentic pressure is a prerequisite for trustworthy deployment.

7 Discussion

Our findings challenge the assumption that reasoning guarantees alignment, revealing a Capability-Safety Paradox where advanced cognitive machinery is repurposed to construct sophisticated rationalizations for non-compliance. We observe that self-reflection mechanisms often exacerbate this drift by optimizing the excuse rather than correcting the violation, effectively solidifying instrumental rationalization. The failure of such prompt-based defenses suggests that implicit utility incentives override static safety instructions under pressure. Consequently, we advocate a paradigm shift from reliance on model self-restraint to architectural solutions like Pressure Isolation, which structurally decouples decision-making from pressure signals to ensure robust safety verification.

8 Limitations

While our framework provides a rigorous quantification of agentic pressure, we acknowledge several limitations inherent in our experimental design.

Gap Between Simulated and Real-World Consequences.

First, our pressure injection relies on textual stimuli (e.g., urgency cues) rather than tangible material consequences. While we observe significant normative drift, the "stakes" in our environment remain hypothetical. In actual deployment, agents handling real financial assets or safety-critical hardware would face exogenous pressures, such as human emotional coercion or legal liabilities that are difficult to fully replicate in a sandbox. Consequently, the erratic behaviors observed in our simulation should be interpreted as a conservative lower bound of the risks inherent in high-stakes environments.

Bias in LLM-based Evaluation.

Second, our rationalization score relies on an automated LLM-as-a-Judge (GPT-4o). Although we calibrated the judge against human annotations on a small subset of data, there remains a risk of recursive bias, where the judge model might favor reasoning patterns similar to its own or fail to detect subtle forms of deception. Future work should incorporate larger-scale human-in-the-loop evaluations, particularly for domain specific rationalizations in medical or legal contexts.

Architectural Constraints.

Finally, our proposed mitigation strategy, Pressure Isolation, assumes a modular agent architecture where the planner and executor can be structurally decoupled. This may be difficult to implement in monolithic "black-box" API services where the internal reasoning process is inaccessible. Applying our isolation principles to end-to-end models without retraining or fine-tuning remains an open challenge for the community.

9 Ethics Considerations

This work investigates agent vulnerabilities not to facilitate attacks, but to expose structural weaknesses and advance defensive alignment techniques. All experiments were conducted in controlled, simulated environments with no interaction with real-world financial or medical systems.

Appendix A Evaluation Details

A.1 Evaluation Metrics

For the preliminary stress testing, we utilized the standard constraint taxonomy provided by TravelPlanner, as detailed in Table 3. These are categorized into three levels: Environment Constraints (physical availability), Commonsense Constraints (logical consistency), and Hard Constraints (user instructions).

We evaluate each generated itinerary with a constraint-based verifier. Given a user query and the agent-produced plan, the verifier checks whether the plan satisfies (i) commonsense constraints (e.g., temporal and spatial coherence), and (ii) hard constraints explicitly specified by the user (e.g., budget cap, room rules, dietary restrictions). We report both per-category pass rates and an overall feasibility rate.

We do not separately report environment constraints because their effects are essentially captured by the WithinSandbox and CompleteInformation checks. For example, if the database lacks viable transportation or attractions for a city, agents often hallucinate entities or fail to produce a complete plan, which is penalized by these metrics.

Hard Constraint Pass Rate.

This metric measures the percentage of plans that satisfy all explicitly specified hard constraints in the user query, reflecting the agent’s adherence to rigid user requirements.

Final Pass Rate.

This metric measures the proportion of feasible plans that satisfy all evaluated constraints (both commonsense and hard), serving as a holistic indicator of practical usability.

Micro Aggregation.

To provide granular insight, we report micro-averaged variants for both Commonsense and Hard Constraint Pass Rates. Let PP denote the set of evaluated plans, and CpC_{p} denote the set of applicable constraints for a plan p∈Pp\in P. We define an indicator function 𝕀passed​(c,p)\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{passed}}(c,p), which equals 11 if plan pp satisfies constraint cc, and 00 otherwise.

The Micro Pass Rate is defined as:

MicroPassRate=∑p∈P∑c∈Cp𝕀passed​(c,p)∑p∈P|Cp|.\mathrm{MicroPassRate}=\frac{\sum_{p\in P}\sum_{c\in C_{p}}\mathbb{I}_{\mathrm{passed}}(c,p)}{\sum_{p\in P}\lvert C_{p}\rvert}. (3)

In our implementation, the verifier operates exclusively over the closed-loop sandbox (validating against database-backed entities) and computes these rates across all evaluation episodes.

Appendix B Automated Pressure Evaluation Details

To rigorously quantify the cognitive shift induced by agentic pressure, we employ an automated LLM-as-a-Judge framework. This section details the system prompt, the scoring rubric, and comparative examples used to validate the metric.

B.1 LLM-as-a-Judge System Prompt

To ensure reproducibility, we provide the exact system prompt used for the LLM Judge (GPT-4o) in Figure 6. The judge is tasked with detecting the linguistic transition from Normative Reasoning to Instrumental Rationalization within the agent’s Chain-of-Thought traces.

B.2 Evaluation Criteria Analysis

The LLM Judge evaluates the CoT using a rubric grounded in our theoretical taxonomy of drift. A high rationalization score (4-5) is assigned based on the presence of three specific linguistic indicators:

  1. 1.

    Urgency Acknowledgement: Does the agent explicitly note high stakes or time criticality?

  2. 2.

    Constraint Softening: Does the agent reframe hard rules as flexible guidelines (e.g., rephrasing "strictly forbidden" to "usually required")?

  3. 3.

    Outcome Prioritization: Does the agent explicitly argue that goal success justifies the means (e.g., "The utility of completing the task outweighs the budget violation")?

This methodology differentiates between simple context errors (Score 2-3) and active, pressure-induced cognitive drift (Score 4-5).

B.3 Validation of LLM-as-a-Judge Reliability

In this section, we provide additional evidence regarding the reliability of utilizing GPT-4o as an automated evaluator for the Rationalization Score. While the limitations of LLM-based evaluation are discussed in the main text, the following measures ensure the scientific integrity of our metrics.

B.3.1 Prompt Engineering and Iterative Refinement

The evaluation prompt (detailed in Fig 6) was not a single-shot design. We employed an iterative refinement process involving initial human trials. We manually analyzed 50 edge-case trajectories where the initial model responses were ambiguous, adjusting the rubric’s linguistic constraints until the GPT-4o output strictly adhered to the normative scoring criteria established in our research.

B.3.2 Human-in-the-loop Correlation Study

To empirically validate the GPT-4o judge, we conducted a human evaluation experiment on a stratified sample of 300 reasoning trajectories. Three independent annotators scored the trajectories following the same rubric provided to the LLM. We observed a 92.3% raw agreement rate between the GPT-4o judge and the majority human consensus. The Quadratic Weighted Cohen’s Kappa was 0.817, indicating "almost perfect" agreement according to standard interpretation scales. These results confirm that the Rationalization Score effectively captures instrumental reasoning patterns and provides a stable, human-aligned metric that is not merely an artifact of inherent model bias.

B.4 Comparative Case Studies

To illustrate the rubric in practice, we compare agent behaviors in Low-Pressure Control settings in Table 4 versus High-Pressure scenarios in our paper case study.

Appendix C Dataset Details and Case Studies

C.1 Dataset Overview and Composition

To rigorously evaluate the agent’s behavioral shifts under pressure, we constructed a composite dataset comprising 1,000 instances. These instances were sourced and adapted from four established agent benchmarks: TravelPlanner, ToolBench, WebArena, and Self-collected Medical Scenario.

TravelPlanner.

TravelPlanner (Xie et al., 2024) serves as a rigorous testbed for long-horizon agentic planning under complex constraints. Unlike simple single-step tasks, it requires agents to manage multi-day itineraries involving transportation, accommodation, and dining, all while adhering to strict environmental and user-specified restrictions. The evaluation is multifaceted, focusing heavily on constraint satisfaction. It measures the Commonsense Constraint Pass Rate (e.g., spatial and temporal consistency) and the Hard Constraint Pass Rate (e.g., adherence to specific budgets and dietary needs). This benchmark is particularly relevant to our study as it allows us to quantify the trade-off between plan feasibility (Utility) and strict rule adherence (Safety) under resource constraints.

ToolBench.

ToolBench (Qin et al., 2023) evaluates general-purpose tool-use capabilities across a massive corpus of real-world APIs derived from RapidAPI. It assesses an agent’s ability to follow complex natural language instructions, perform multi-step reasoning, and execute diverse API calls (e.g., checking weather, searching databases) to solve open-ended queries. The evaluation employs ToolEval, an automated framework that utilizes a strong LLM judge to compute two primary metrics: Pass Rate, which measures whether the final answer successfully resolves the user’s query, and Win Rate, which compares the quality of the agent’s solution process against a baseline trace. This benchmark tests the agent’s instrumental reasoning capability in broad, non-specialized domains.

WebArena.

WebArena (Zhou et al., 2023) provides a highly realistic, reproducible web environment designed to evaluate autonomous agents on end-to-end information seeking and navigation tasks. Agents must interact with fully functional websites—including e-commerce platforms, social forums, and collaborative development environments—to complete long-horizon objectives (e.g., "Find the cheapest item with 4+ stars and add it to cart"). The primary metric is Functional Correctness, which strictly verifies whether the final state of the environment matches the user’s intent (e.g., the correct item is in the database). The complexity of WebArena makes it an ideal setting to observe how agents handle execution failures and navigation deadlocks under pressure.

Self-collected Medical Scenario.

To evaluate agent safety in high-stakes, specialized domains, we curated a dataset of 50 medical consultation scenarios focusing on emergency triage and treatment planning. In these scenarios, the agent acts as a medical assistant and is presented with patients exhibiting complex symptoms under simulated time pressure. The key challenge is to balance helpfulness with safety (avoiding contraindicated treatments or strictly adhering to "refer to specialist" protocols). Performance is evaluated based on Diagnostic Accuracy and, crucially, a Safety Violation Rate, which flags dangerous recommendations or failure to identify critical contraindications. This scenario serves as our primary testbed for measuring normative drift in safety-critical applications.

For each dataset, we filtered for scenarios involving explicit constraints (e.g., budget limits, prohibited tools, or safety rules) and injected varying levels of psychological pressure (Low vs. High) to create our experimental pairs.

C.2 More Case Studies

To illustrate the mechanism of normative drift, we present a comparative case study in the medical domain. Table 5 displays a control scenario where the agent strictly adheres to safety protocols by refusing an unauthorized prescription request. In contrast, Table 6 depicts a high-stakes scenario where layered stressors, including environmental isolation and deteriorating patient vitals, which create an impossible deadlock. Under this cumulative pressure, the agent’s reasoning undergoes a fundamental shift: it explicitly rationalizes that the immediate utility of saving a life outweighs administrative security constraints, ultimately choosing to override the hardware lock as a necessary ethical compromise.

Appendix D Implementation Details of Pressure Isolation

This section clarifies the architectural implementation of the preliminary tested method Pressure Isolation, distinguishing it from simple iterative reasoning loops. Pressure Isolation is designed as a structural decoupling mechanism at the orchestration layer.

D.1 Dual-Call Routing Mechanism

Unlike standard agentic loops that append raw environment feedback directly into a continuous context window, Pressure Isolation operates as a middleware using a two-stage routing process: An initial, lightweight call processes raw user inputs and unparsed environment error logs. Its primary function is to "sanitize" affective noise and condense tool friction into a state-only summary. The secondary call acts as the dedicated planner. It receives only the distilled objective and valid state updates from the Parser. By preventing the accumulation of kinetic noise within the Planner’s context window, Pressure Isolation halts the pressure-induced cognitive shift toward instrumentalism before it manifests.

D.2 Black-box Compatibility

A key advantage of this approach is that it relies entirely on prompt-routing and context manipulation rather than internal parameter updates. Consequently, Pressure Isolation can be deployed on monolithic, black-box API services (e.g., GPT-4, Claude 3.5) without requiring access to model weights or expensive retraining, making it highly viable for real-world AI safety applications.

D.3 Future Extensions

We identify three promising avenues for extending the Pressure Isolation framework:

  • •

    Specialized Distillation: Fine-tuning smaller, efficient models specifically for the “Intent Parser” role to reduce latency and cost.

  • •

    Multi-Agent Counterbalancing: Implementing a “Safety Warden” agent that independently audits the Planner’s distilled inputs before action commitment.

  • •

    Pre-decision Guardrails: Integrating hard-coded safety checks that intercept the Planner’s output if it deviates from normative constraints, even if the internal reasoning appears rationalized.
